Family Health

How leukemia is diagnosed: symptoms, tests, types and next steps

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Leukemia is a group of cancers affecting blood-forming cells. Symptoms or an unexpected blood-test result may start an investigation, but no single symptom checklist can confirm it. The important next step is to identify the exact type and the features that guide care. Some leukemias need urgent treatment; others may initially be monitored closely.

What changes in the blood and bone marrow?

Bone marrow contains cells that develop into red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets. Red cells carry oxygen, white cells contribute to immune defence, and platelets help stop bleeding. Leukemia usually involves abnormal cells in a white-cell lineage, although the disease can disrupt production of all three groups.

Abnormal cells may accumulate and crowd out healthy blood formation. A high white-cell count does not necessarily mean strong immunity: leukemia cells may not work normally. Some people instead have low or near-normal total white counts. Interpretation depends on which cells are present and what the rest of the blood results show.

White cells are part of a wider immune system

Different white cells help protect against bacteria, viruses, fungi and abnormal cells. Blood-forming stem cells originate in the marrow; immune-cell maturation and activity also involve tissues such as the thymus, lymph nodes and spleen. Blood and lymphatic circulation help immune cells reach where they are needed.

This explains why a blood cancer can affect lymph nodes or the spleen as well as a blood count. It does not mean that every swollen node is leukemia. Nodes often enlarge during ordinary infections, and a clinician considers the pattern, duration, examination and test results together.

Symptoms that deserve an assessment

Possible symptoms include persistent unusual tiredness or weakness, fever or chills, drenching night sweats, unexplained weight loss and repeated infections. Easy bruising, bleeding or pinpoint red or purple spots called petechiae can reflect low platelets. Painless lumps, especially in the neck or underarm, may be enlarged lymph nodes.

An enlarged liver or spleen can cause abdominal discomfort or fullness. Anaemia may contribute to breathlessness or fatigue. These findings have other possible causes and are not a diagnosis by themselves. Arrange assessment for unexplained, persistent or worsening changes rather than waiting for every symptom on a list to appear.

When symptoms need urgent help

Severe breathing difficulty, uncontrolled bleeding, a new seizure, sudden confusion or new weakness needs emergency assessment. Headache, vomiting or balance changes can have many causes, but new or severe neurological symptoms should not be assessed through an online checklist.

For someone already diagnosed or receiving treatment, fever or new illness may need immediate contact with the cancer team. Follow the team’s specific emergency plan, including its temperature threshold and contact number. Waiting for a routine appointment can be unsafe when infection-fighting cells are low.

Organ involvement depends on the leukemia type

Leukemia cells can involve sites beyond the blood and marrow, including lymph nodes, liver, spleen, skin or, in some types, the central nervous system and testicles. Symptoms involving the lungs, digestive tract, heart or kidneys may also need investigation, but do not automatically mean that leukemia cells have entered that organ.

The word metastasis can be confusing here. Leukemia does not follow one universal solid-tumour pathway from a local lump to stage IV disease. Doctors choose tests according to the subtype, symptoms and treatment plan. They also look for other explanations, such as infection, anaemia or treatment effects.

Two distinctions help organize the main types

Acute leukemias typically involve immature cells and can progress quickly without treatment. Chronic forms often have a more gradual course, but “chronic” does not mean harmless or that treatment is never needed. The cell lineage also matters: lymphoid cells develop into lymphocytes, whereas myeloid lineages include several other blood-cell types.

Combining these distinctions gives four familiar names: acute myeloid leukemia, acute lymphoblastic leukemia, chronic myeloid leukemia and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Each group contains further biological differences. A report naming the subtype and its genetic features is more informative than the word leukemia alone.

Acute myeloid leukemia: AML

AML can occur in children or adults and is the most common acute leukemia in adults. It is not the most common leukemia in every population. Subtypes matter greatly; acute promyelocytic leukemia, for example, has particular bleeding risks and a different treatment approach. Suspected acute leukemia warrants prompt specialist assessment.

For context, the NCI SEER table projects 22,720 new US AML cases in 2026 and reports five-year relative survival of 33.4% for 2016–2022. Those are population figures covering varied ages and disease biology. They do not predict the outcome of a particular person starting treatment now.

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia: ALL

ALL, also called acute lymphocytic leukemia, affects the lymphoid lineage. It is particularly important in childhood cancer but also occurs in adults. Testing distinguishes B-cell and T-cell disease and looks for genetic changes that may affect treatment. Age-specific treatment and response make a substantial difference to outlook.

SEER projects 6,250 new US ALL cases in 2026 and reports five-year relative survival of 73.2% for 2016–2022 across ages. This combined figure must not be presented as the chance of survival for an individual child or adult. The treating team can explain which evidence best matches the person’s situation.

Chronic myeloid leukemia: CML

CML mainly affects adults and is characterized by the BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, usually associated with the Philadelphia chromosome. This abnormal signal provides a target for medicines called tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Imatinib is one example, alongside other options selected according to disease features, response and health considerations.

SEER projects 9,650 new US CML cases in 2026 and reports five-year relative survival of 71.1% for 2016–2022. Modern treatment has changed the course of CML for many people. Regular molecular monitoring remains important even when symptoms are absent or blood counts improve.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia and hairy cell leukemia

CLL usually occurs in older adults and is exceptionally uncommon in children. Some people have few symptoms and are diagnosed after a routine blood test. Selected patients can be monitored before treatment is needed. SEER projects 22,760 new US cases in 2026 and reports five-year relative survival of 90.2% for 2016–2022.

Hairy cell leukemia is a separate, uncommon B-cell malignancy, not a subtype of CLL. Its name describes the appearance of affected cells under a microscope. Although it can also behave slowly, its diagnostic markers and management differ. Similar-sounding names should not be used to transfer one person’s treatment plan to another.

Risk factors are not a verdict about the cause

Relevant risk factors vary by subtype. They can include previous chemotherapy or radiation treatment, high-dose ionizing radiation exposure, certain inherited conditions such as Down syndrome, and particular blood disorders including myelodysplastic syndromes. Smoking and benzene exposure are associated with AML risk.

A family history can matter, particularly for CLL or specific inherited predispositions, but most diagnoses do not mean that a parent directly passed on leukemia. Many affected people have no identifiable risk factor. Give the team an accurate health, treatment, occupational and family history without assuming that one exposure proves why the cancer developed.

The first visit and blood tests

A clinician asks about symptoms, previous illnesses and treatments, medicines and family history, and examines areas such as the lymph nodes and abdomen. A complete blood count, or CBC, measures red cells, white cells and platelets. A differential separates white-cell types, and a blood smear allows their appearance to be examined.

These tests can identify a concerning pattern, but one high count alone does not confirm leukemia. Infection and other conditions can change blood counts too. If results suggest a blood cancer, referral is usually to a hematologist, often a hematologist-oncologist, who arranges the tests needed to establish the precise diagnosis.

What a bone-marrow sample adds

Bone-marrow aspiration removes a small amount of liquid marrow; a core biopsy samples a small piece of marrow-containing tissue. The hip bone is a common site. The team explains pain relief, possible sedation, bleeding precautions and aftercare. Laboratory specialists examine the cells and may use the sample for several additional tests.

Marrow testing is often important in acute leukemia, but it is not mandatory for every person with every leukemia. CLL can frequently be diagnosed from blood tests, including the appropriate cell-marker analysis. A lymph-node biopsy may be useful in selected circumstances; liver or spleen biopsy is not a routine requirement for everyone.

Flow cytometry and genetic tests answer different questions

Flow cytometry helps identify cells by their characteristics and marker patterns, a process called immunophenotyping. It can help distinguish one leukemia from another. It should not be described simply as a test that reads DNA and calculates how fast a cancer is growing.

Cytogenetic analysis examines chromosomes, while FISH and molecular tests look for particular rearrangements or gene changes. Findings can guide treatment selection and later monitoring. Some results arrive later than the initial blood count. Ask which findings are already known, which are pending and whether any immediate care must start before the complete report is available.

Lumbar puncture, scans and organ-function tests

A lumbar puncture collects cerebrospinal fluid through a needle in the lower back when assessment of the brain and spinal-cord fluid is relevant. It is particularly important in some ALL plans and may also be used to deliver treatment. It is not a routine test for every leukemia subtype; the team assesses its indication and safety.

Imaging such as ultrasound, CT or an x-ray can investigate enlarged organs, nodes or specific symptoms. Liver and kidney blood tests help assess overall health and treatment safety, but an abnormal liver result alone does not prove leukemia infiltration. Scans and chemistry tests complement cell-based diagnosis rather than replacing it.

Why there is no single leukemia staging system

AML and ALL are not assigned a standard stage I–IV in the way many solid cancers are. Clinicians consider subtype, genetics, disease sites, risk group and whether disease is newly diagnosed, in remission, resistant or recurrent. The number of white cells may contribute to a risk assessment without constituting a universal stage.

CLL uses systems such as Rai or Binet, incorporating blood-cell findings and enlarged lymphoid organs. CML is described by disease phase; classifications differ in their use of an accelerated phase between chronic and blast phases. Ask the team which system appears in your report and what it changes about care, rather than comparing stage labels across leukemia types.

Why some people start treatment and others are monitored

A plan depends on the exact disease, genetic results, symptoms, response so far, age, overall health and personal priorities. Acute leukemia often needs prompt treatment. Selected people with asymptomatic CLL or another indolent disease may instead have scheduled examinations and blood tests until there is a reason to treat.

Active monitoring is a clinical strategy, not abandonment. It should include follow-up dates and clear instructions about new symptoms. The idea that treatment is always better simply because it starts earlier is not correct for every leukemia. Do not delay urgent acute-leukemia care by applying advice intended for stable CLL.

Chemotherapy, targeted therapy and immunotherapy

Chemotherapy uses medicines that kill or inhibit cancer cells and may involve combinations and several treatment phases. Targeted medicines act on particular cancer-cell features; a BCR::ABL1 inhibitor for CML is one example. Immunotherapies help direct immune activity against the cancer, including antibody-based treatments and, for selected situations, cellular therapies.

These categories can overlap or be combined. Availability and suitability differ by subtype and country. The team also manages infection risk, blood-cell shortages and other effects, sometimes with transfusions or anti-infective medicines. Ask what each part of the plan is intended to accomplish and which side effects need an immediate call.

When radiation or stem-cell transplantation is considered

Radiation uses high-energy beams to treat selected areas; in some transplant programmes, total-body irradiation forms part of preparation. It is not a routine treatment for every leukemia. Its role depends on the disease, sites involved, age and wider treatment plan.

A stem-cell transplant restores blood formation using an infusion of blood-forming cells after preparatory treatment. It does not involve surgically swapping out all the bone marrow. Donor cells are used in many leukemia transplants; use of a person’s own cells is limited to selected settings. Benefits and serious risks require an individual specialist discussion.

Understand what survival statistics can and cannot say

Five-year relative survival compares survival after cancer with that expected in a similar general population. It is not a five-year deadline or a guarantee of cure. The figures above use US SEER data for 2016–2022; the 2026 case estimates are separate projections. All-age averages can hide large differences in biology, access to care and treatment response.

Across leukemia types, SEER reports five-year relative survival of 68.6% for 2016–2022. It also reports an average annual decline of 1.8% in age-adjusted death rates during 2015–2024. These population trends are encouraging context, not a prediction for one family. Ask for an outlook based on the actual subtype and current treatment options.

Prepare for the next conversation with the care team

Ask for the exact diagnosis in writing, which tests are still pending, the aim of treatment and the timeline for the next decision. Keep a copy of the blood results and pathology report. A second opinion can help clarify complex decisions, but coordinate it with the treating team so urgent care is not delayed.

As treatment progresses, response (including measurable residual disease testing when appropriate) may change the discussion about risk. Ask about practical support, fertility or pregnancy concerns when relevant, and how to contact the team outside office hours. For a child, the pediatric oncology team will explain the plan in age-appropriate terms and help the family manage day-to-day needs.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI and cancer-society guidance distinguish cell-based diagnosis, subtype-specific risk assessment and treatment. Flow cytometry, chromosome testing, molecular analysis, imaging and organ-function tests have different purposes; they cannot be substituted for one another.

The statistical examples are dated US population data, checked against SEER, and do not estimate an individual outcome. Phase definitions and treatment options evolve, so the treating hematology team must interpret the exact classification and current local guidance.

How BeMama can help

Keep one written list of the diagnosis, pending results, next appointment and urgent contact instructions so family members are working from the same information.

When to seek help

This overview cannot diagnose leukemia. Seek emergency help for severe breathing difficulty, uncontrolled bleeding or new severe neurological symptoms, and follow the cancer team’s urgent fever instructions during treatment.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Leukemia includes several different diseases; symptoms or one blood count cannot identify the type.
  • Blood, marrow, cell-marker and genetic tests guide diagnosis and treatment, with other tests selected as needed.
  • Acute leukemia often needs urgent care, while selected chronic disease may be monitored first.
  • Dated survival statistics describe populations and must not be used as a personal forecast.

Frequently asked questions

Does a high white-cell count always mean leukemia?

No. Infection and other conditions can raise the count. Leukemia can also occur without a high total count, so clinicians interpret the cell types, other blood results and clinical situation together.

Can leukemia be diagnosed from symptoms alone?

No. Fatigue, bruising, fever and swollen nodes have several possible causes. Persistent or concerning changes need assessment and appropriate testing.

Will everyone need a bone-marrow biopsy?

No. It is often important in acute leukemia, but some types, including many cases of CLL, can be diagnosed from appropriate blood tests. Your team will explain why a sample is or is not needed.

Is flow cytometry the same as a genetic test?

No. It commonly identifies cell-marker patterns. Chromosome analysis, FISH and molecular tests examine different features and may provide additional information for classification and treatment.

Does an abnormal liver test prove the leukemia has spread?

No. Liver tests can change for many reasons. The team interprets them alongside symptoms, medicines, examination and any indicated imaging or further tests.

What stage is leukemia?

There is no one staging system for all leukemias. AML and ALL use subtype and risk information rather than standard solid-tumour stages; CLL and CML have their own staging or phase frameworks.

Is hairy cell leukemia a type of CLL?

No. It is a separate B-cell malignancy with its own diagnostic characteristics and treatment considerations.

Why might a doctor recommend monitoring instead of immediate treatment?

Selected slow-growing disease, such as some asymptomatic CLL, may not benefit from immediate treatment. Monitoring must be planned and supervised; this advice does not apply to urgent acute-leukemia care.

Does five-year survival mean a person has only five years to live?

No. It is a statistical follow-up measure, not a time limit. Many people live much longer, and an individual outlook depends on disease biology, health and treatment response.

What should we ask when results are still coming back?

Ask what is confirmed, which subtype or genetic results remain pending, whether any care must begin now, and whom to contact if symptoms change. Request a written next-step and emergency plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
